passage: Disha knew her weak spot: the library was quiet, but her phone was not, and Arohi could talk her into chai and a walk in under a minute. So before exam week she wrote a line on a sticky note. "If Arohi asks me out while I'm studying, I'll say 'later, at six', and go then." On Tuesday Arohi leaned over her desk and whispered, "Coffee?" Disha grinned, said, "Later, at six," and turned back to her notes. At six they had coffee, and she felt no guilt at all. At twenty-five, Disha kept saying she would stretch her stiff back every day. The idea never lasted past Wednesday. Then she made a small change: right after brushing her teeth, still at the sink, she would bend forward and hang there for a few breaths. Within two weeks she did it without thinking. Her flatmate Ramesh once walked in and asked, "Are you meditating in the bathroom?" She laughed. "No. Toothbrush, then stretch. It's just what comes next."

qa.q: What did Disha say when Arohi invited her for coffee in the library?
How does the plan Disha made as a student differ from the plan she made as a working adult?
qa.a: As a student she planned for an obstacle, deciding in advance what to say when Arohi asked her out during study hours, and went at six. Later she tied a new action, stretching, to the old habit of brushing her teeth so it happened without her deciding.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when she went for coffee at six?
qa.a: She felt content and free of guilt, because she had already kept her promise to study first.

qa.q: What could Disha do if her stretching again drops off?
qa.a: She could look at what comes right before it, such as brushing her teeth, and keep the stretch on that same spot, perhaps with a note on the mirror.

grounding: One person's intentions hold at two ages: by planning what to do when a distraction arrives and by attaching a new action to an existing routine.
